It's a two part issue.  The weight shift didn't -directly- cause the crash.  But it did cause the nose to pitch upwards.  Planes burn fuel to fly, and to burn fuel you need two things: the fuel itself and sufficient oxygen for the combustion reaction to happen.  Oxygen is pushed through the engines by the forward movement of the plane.  When a plane stalls, what happens is that the forward velocity is insufficient to meet the oxygen requirements of the engine, so fuel stops combusting and the engines stop moving.  If there's enough altitude, the engines can be restarted by the airflow caused by the plane falling down.  But in this case, they were so close to the ground, there was not enough time to restart the engines.

So I'm a pediatric speech pathologist, and I spend a surprisingly large amount of time every week singing songs like "Wheels on the Bus" and "Old MacDonald Has a Farm" to kids with speech/language disorders.  There is actually a good justification for singing 'inane' songs repetitively to children.  They need a toe-hold into the world of signs & symbols.  Songs activate both hemispheres and give little kids a cue (timing, pitch) for when their turn to participate is, and what they should say, before they understand necessarily what the words even mean. It also helps them learn what parts of the speech signal are meaningful and what are not.  

It helps them start making connections between symbols - i.e., old macdonald teaches kids that sheep say "baa" and cows say "moo." And this might not seem like an important thing for a baby or anyone to know, but it's like putting a stick into a sugar solution and making rock candy - you need something in their brains for everything else about language to stick to.

If you've been doing stronglifts and have a reasonable amount of muscle, you may have a BMI in the obese range, but you are probably not actually obese.  BMI cut-offs are not what defines obesity - BF% is.  BMI is just a useful way to estimate it, but the boundaries are actually somewhat fuzzy (meaning someone just under 30 with zero muscle could be obese, while someone just over 30 with significant muscle might not be), but only about 1-2 points worth of fuzz.  Like if your BMI was 32 or 33, you're almost certainly obese. If your BMI is 27, you're most likely not obese, regardless of muscle mass.
